title: Linear Equation Solving by Elimination
body:
Linear equation solving by elimination is the school and workshop method for finding the values that satisfy a set of linear equations at once. Two equations in two unknowns describe two straight lines, and the solution is the point where they cross. Elimination works by adding or subtracting scaled copies of the equations so that one unknown cancels, leaving a single equation that can be solved directly, after which the second unknown follows by substitution. The method needs no guessing and no special device, only careful arithmetic, which is why it has survived every change in calculating technology.

Method. The working method for this record is Gaussian elimination applied to a two-equation system. First, the equations are written in the same order of unknowns so like terms line up. Second, one equation is scaled so that the coefficient of the unknown to be removed matches the other equation. Third, the equations are added or subtracted to cancel that unknown, and the surviving equation is solved. Fourth, the found value is substituted back into either original equation to recover the other unknown. Fifth, both values are checked by inserting them into both original equations, because a solution that fails either check is not a solution.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for linear equation solving by elimination. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: x: 2.0; y: 1.0; check eq1: True; check eq2: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a problem reduces to straight-line relationships, such as mixing two quantities to a target total, splitting a fixed budget between two items, or converting between two related measures. Do not use it where the relationships curve or multiply together, because elimination on its own cannot solve nonlinear systems, and do not trust a result that has not been checked in both original equations. title: Sudoku Constraint Propagation
body:
Sudoku constraint propagation is the method by which a Sudoku puzzle is solved without guessing: every empty cell carries a set of candidate digits, and the rules of the puzzle steadily shrink those sets until only one digit can fit. A digit is impossible in a cell when it already appears in the same row, the same column, or the same small box, so each placed digit removes candidates from its whole row, column, and box. When only one candidate remains for a cell, that digit is forced, and placing it starts a new round of removals. Puzzles that resist pure propagation are finished by trying a candidate and backtracking when the trial contradicts the rules.

Method. The working method for this record is candidate elimination followed by backtracking on a four by four grid, where each row, column, and two by two box must contain the digits one through four exactly once. First, the given digits are placed and every empty cell's candidate set is reduced by its row, column, and box. Second, any cell reduced to a single candidate is filled, and the reduction repeats. Third, when no cell is forced, the search tries a candidate in the emptiest cell and continues; if a contradiction appears, it returns to the last choice and tries the next candidate. Fourth, the finished grid is checked against all row, column, and box rules before it is accepted.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for sudoku constraint propagation. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 1 2 3 4; 3 4 1 2; 2 1 4 3; 4 3 2 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a puzzle or scheduling problem is really a set of all-different constraints, such as assigning distinct values to a row of slots or checking that a placement breaks no rule. Do not use it as a claim that every puzzle yields to propagation alone, because some puzzles genuinely need search, and do not accept a grid that has not been checked against every row, column, and box. title: Binary Search
body:
Binary search is the method for finding an item in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search space instead of scanning from the start. Because the list is sorted, comparing the target with the middle item tells the searcher which half can contain it, and the other half is discarded without being examined. Each step halves the remaining candidates, so a list of a thousand items needs at most ten comparisons, and a list of a million needs at most twenty. The method is one of the oldest and most used ideas in computing, and it is the reason sorted indexes answer questions so quickly.

Method. The working method for this record is binary search on a sorted list of numbers. First, the lowest and highest candidate positions are set to the ends of the list. Second, the middle position is computed and its value compared with the target. Third, if the middle value equals the target, the search stops with its position. Fourth, if the middle value is smaller, the lower bound moves past the middle, and if larger, the upper bound moves before it. Fifth, the loop repeats until the target is found or the bounds cross, which proves the target is absent. Every probe is counted so the efficiency of the method is visible in the output.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for binary search. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: target: 41; found at index: 7; probes: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record whenever the data is sorted or can be sorted once and searched many times, such as looking up a word in a dictionary, a record in an index, or a setting in a sorted table. Do not use it on unsorted data, where it gives wrong answers, and do not use it where the cost of sorting outweighs a single lookup. found = -1

    probes += 1

    else:

title: Morse Code Decoding
body:
Morse code decoding is the method for turning sequences of short and long signals into letters. Each letter is a short pattern of dots and dashes: three dots make S, three dashes make O, and the distress signal SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots. Letters are separated by a short gap and words by a longer gap, which in written form is shown with spaces between letters and a slash between words. The code was designed so the most common letters have the shortest patterns, which keeps messages compact, and it remains readable by ear, by light, and by touch.

Method. The working method for this record is table lookup decoding of written Morse symbols. First, the message is split into words on the slash separator. Second, each word is split into letter symbols on spaces. Third, each symbol is looked up in the standard Morse table to recover its letter. Fourth, the letters are joined into words and the words into the message. Fifth, any symbol that is not in the table is reported as unknown rather than guessed, because a guessed letter corrupts the whole message. The demo decodes a short two-word message with this exact procedure.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for morse code decoding. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: decoded: SOS THE Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a signal arrives as dots and dashes, whether by sound, flashing light, or written symbols, and when the message must be recovered exactly rather than approximately. Do not use it for codes it does not describe, such as other telegraph alphabets, and do not guess unknown symbols. title: Base64 Decoding
body:
Base64 decoding is the method for recovering original bytes from text that was encoded so binary data could travel through text-only channels. The encoding represents every three bytes as four characters drawn from letters, digits, plus, and slash, with equals signs padding the end when the byte count is not a multiple of three. Decoding reverses the process: each character contributes six bits, the bits are regrouped into bytes, and padding characters are discarded. The result is the exact original data, which is why Base64 is used for attachments, embedded images, and data sent inside text formats.

Method. The working method for this record is standard Base64 decoding with the Python standard library. First, the encoded text is checked for valid Base64 characters and padding. Second, each group of four characters is converted back into three bytes through its six-bit values. Third, padding characters at the end reduce the final group to one or two bytes as appropriate. Fourth, the recovered bytes are decoded as text and printed. Fifth, the result is compared with the known original word, so the demo proves the round trip rather than merely asserting it.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for base64 decoding. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record whenever data arrives Base64-encoded and must be recovered exactly, such as reading an encoded field out of a text file or checking what an encoded string contains. Do not use it for encrypted data, which Base64 does not protect, and do not treat a decoded result as meaningful until its own format is checked. title: OBD-II Trouble Code Lookup
body:
OBD-II trouble code lookup is the method for turning a diagnostic code from a vehicle's onboard computer into a plain description of the fault it detected. Since 1996, vehicles sold in the United States carry an OBD-II port, and when the engine computer detects a fault it stores a five-character code: a letter for the system, a digit for whether the code is standard or manufacturer-specific, and three digits for the fault family and the specific fault. A code reader displays the code, and the lookup table gives the standard meaning, which tells the mechanic which system to inspect first without guessing.

Method. The working method for this record is dictionary lookup against the standard SAE code meanings. First, the code's leading letter is read: P means powertrain, which covers engine and transmission faults. Second, the code is matched exactly in the lookup table, because near matches are different faults. Third, the standard meaning is returned together with the system it belongs to. Fourth, the record states plainly that the code names the system and the detected condition, not the failed part, since several parts can produce the same code. The demo looks up three widely documented powertrain codes and prints their standard meanings.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for obd-ii trouble code lookup. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: P0300: Random/multiple cylinder misfire detected; P0171: System too lean (bank 1); P0420: Catalyst system efficiency below threshold (bank 1) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a code reader has produced a code and the next step is to understand which system reported a fault and what condition it detected. Do not use it as a repair instruction on its own, because a code points at a system to test, not at a part to replace, and do not clear codes before the fault is understood. title: A-Star Pathfinding
body:
A-star pathfinding is the method for finding the cheapest route across a grid or a map by balancing what a route has already cost against a reasoned estimate of what remains. Each candidate square carries two numbers: the cost of the best route found to it so far, and a heuristic estimate of the distance from it to the goal, usually the straight-line or Manhattan distance. The search always expands the square with the lowest sum of the two, which keeps it from wandering while still guaranteeing the cheapest route whenever the heuristic never overestimates. The method drives game characters, robot navigation, and route planning.

Method. The working method for this record is A-star search on a five by five grid with four-directional movement and a Manhattan distance heuristic. First, the start square is placed in the open set with a cost of zero. Second, the open square with the lowest sum of travelled cost and heuristic is expanded, and each reachable neighbor is given a travelled cost one higher. Third, a neighbor that is reached more cheaply than before has its record updated and its previous square remembered. Fourth, when the goal square is expanded, the remembered links are followed back to reconstruct the route. Fifth, the route and its total cost are printed, and the cost is checked against the Manhattan distance lower bound.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for a-star pathfinding. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: path: (0, 0) -> (0, 1) -> (0, 2) -> (0, 3) -> (0, 4) -> (1, 4) -> (2, 4) -> (3, 4) -> (4, 4); cost: 8 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a route must be cheapest, not merely passable, and when a reasonable distance estimate exists, such as grid movement, road maps, or puzzle states. Do not use it with a heuristic that overestimates, because the cheapest-route guarantee then fails, and do not use it where the cheapest route is not the goal. title: Newton's Method for Root Finding
body:
Newton's method is the iterative method for finding a number whose function value is zero, which includes square roots, cube roots, and the solutions of many equations that cannot be rearranged by hand. Starting from a guess, the method draws the tangent line to the function's curve at the guess and takes where that line crosses zero as the next guess. Each step typically doubles the number of correct digits, so a handful of iterations reaches high accuracy. The method needs the function's derivative and a starting guess close enough that the tangent lines lead toward the root rather than away from it.

Method. The working method for this record is Newton iteration for the square root of two, solving x squared minus two equals zero. First, the function and its derivative, two times x, are stated. Second, a starting guess of one is chosen. Third, each iteration replaces the guess with the guess minus the function value divided by the derivative, which is the tangent-line crossing. Fourth, five iterations are performed and each new guess is printed to six decimal places. Fifth, the final guess is squared and compared with two, showing the error the iteration has reached.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for newton's method for root finding. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: iteration 1: 1.500000; iteration 2: 1.416667; iteration 3: 1.414216; iteration 4: 1.414214; iteration 5: 1.414214; squared: 2.000000 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when an equation has a smooth function and a derivative and a reasonable starting guess, such as roots, calibration constants, and inverse calculations. Do not use it where the derivative is zero at the guess, where the function jumps, or where the starting guess is far from any root, because the iteration can then diverge or cycle. title: Least Squares Line Fitting
body:
Least squares line fitting is the method for drawing the straight line that best summarizes a scatter of points, where best means the line that makes the total squared vertical distance from the points to the line as small as possible. Squaring the distances keeps positive and negative misses from cancelling and punishes large misses more than small ones, which matches how a summary line should behave. The slope and intercept come from closed-form sums over the data, so the fit is computed exactly rather than searched for, and the same sums produce the line for any number of points.

Method. The working method for this record is ordinary least squares for a line y equals a plus b times x. First, the sums of x, y, x times y, and x squared are accumulated over the four data points. Second, the slope is computed as the number of points times the sum of x times y minus the sum of x times the sum of y, divided by the number of points times the sum of x squared minus the square of the sum of x. Third, the intercept is computed as the mean of y minus the slope times the mean of x. Fourth, the fitted line is printed together with the predicted value at each x, so the fit can be inspected point by point.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for least squares line fitting. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: slope: 1.1000; intercept: 1.1000; x=0 actual=1 fitted=1.1000; x=1 actual=3 fitted=2.2000; x=2 actual=2 fitted=3.3000; x=3 actual=5 fitted=4.4000 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a relationship looks straight and a single summary line is wanted, such as calibration curves, trend estimates, and simple forecasts. Do not use it where the relationship curves strongly, where outliers dominate the squares, or where the line will be extended far beyond the data, because the fit only describes the range it was computed from. title: Crossword Pattern Matching
body:
Crossword pattern matching is the method for solving a crossword clue's pattern by filtering a word list to the words that fit the known letters. A pattern uses question marks for unknown letters, so a pattern like C question K question matches any four-letter word with C first and K third. The matcher walks the list once, keeps the words whose letters agree with every known position and whose length matches the pattern, and returns the survivors as candidates. The solver then uses the clue's meaning and the crossing words to choose among them, which is why a good matcher returns all fits rather than guessing one.

Method. The working method for this record is straightforward pattern filtering over a small built-in word list. First, the pattern and the word list are stated. Second, each word is kept only when its length equals the pattern length. Third, each known letter in the pattern is compared with the same position in the word, and any disagreement discards the word. Fourth, the surviving words are printed together with their count. Fifth, the procedure is repeated for a second pattern to show that the same code answers different patterns without change.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for crossword pattern matching. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record when a word puzzle gives a length and some letters, or when any list must be filtered by a letter pattern, such as anagrams with fixed positions or code words with known characters. title: Rubik's Cube Layer Method Notation
body:
Rubik's cube layer method notation is the written language for cube algorithms, and reading it is the first skill every cube solver learns. Each face has a letter: R for right, L for left, U for up, D for down, F for front, and B for back. A bare letter turns that face a quarter turn clockwise as seen facing the face, a letter followed by an apostrophe turns it a quarter turn counterclockwise, and a letter followed by two turns it halfway. Algorithms are sequences of such moves, and the beginner's layer method strings them into steps that solve the cube layer by layer: first the cross, then the first-layer corners, then the second layer, then the last layer.

Method. The working method for this record is parsing Singmaster notation into a counted move list. First, the algorithm string is split into tokens on spaces. Second, each token is checked against the six face letters with an optional apostrophe or two suffix. The demo parses notation only; it does not claim a cube state, which would need a full cube model.

title: Fault Isolation by Half-Splitting
body:
Fault isolation by half-splitting is the diagnostic method for finding a single faulty segment in a chain by testing the middle instead of testing every segment in order. The method relies on one condition: segments before the fault test good and segments from the fault onward test faulty, so a single test at the middle tells the searcher which half contains the fault. Each test halves the suspect range, so an eight-segment chain needs at most three tests and a thousand-segment chain needs at most ten. The same idea locates bad commits in software history, bad sections in a pipeline, and bad stages in a process line.

Method. The working method for this record is binary search for the first faulty segment in an eight-segment chain with the fault at segment five. First, the test function is defined: it reports faulty for segments at or after the fault and good before it. Second, the low and high bounds are set to the ends of the chain. Third, the middle segment is tested; a good result moves the low bound past the middle, and a faulty result moves the high bound to the middle. Fourth, the loop repeats until the bounds meet, which is the faulty segment. Fifth, every probe and the final answer are printed so the halving is visible.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for fault isolation by half-splitting. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: probes: [3, 5, 4]; faulty segment: 5 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a chain has a monotone fault boundary, meaning one fault makes everything downstream test faulty, such as a broken conductor in a series line or a bad stage in a pipeline. Do not use it where several independent faults exist or where the test itself is unreliable, because the halving logic then points at the wrong segment. title: Constraint Satisfaction by Backtracking
body:
Constraint satisfaction by backtracking is the general method for placing items under rules that forbid certain combinations, and the four-queens puzzle is its classic demonstration. Four queens must be placed on a four by four board so that no two share a row, a column, or a diagonal, which means each row holds exactly one queen and each new queen must avoid the columns and diagonals of the queens already placed. Backtracking places queens row by row, and when a row has no safe column it returns to the previous row and moves that queen to its next safe column. The search is exhaustive, so when it reports a board, the board satisfies every rule.

Method. The working method for this record is row-by-row backtracking for four queens. First, queens are placed one row at a time, tracking used columns and both diagonal directions. Second, a candidate column is accepted only when its column and both diagonals are free. Third, when a row has no safe column, the search backtracks to the previous row and advances that queen. Fourth, when all four rows hold queens, the board is complete and the search stops at the first solution. Fifth, the solution is printed as column positions per row and as a board picture, and the board is verified against the row, column, and diagonal rules.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for constraint satisfaction by backtracking. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: queen columns per row: [1, 3, 0, 2]; .Q..; ...Q; Q...; ..Q. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a problem is a set of placements under all-different and diagonal-style rules, such as scheduling with conflicts, map coloring, and puzzle solving. Do not use it where the search space is enormous without added propagation, because pure backtracking then takes too long, and do not accept a placement that has not been checked against every rule. title: Dynamic Programming for Shortest Route
body:
Dynamic programming for the shortest route solves a routing problem by working through its stages in order and remembering the best cost to each point, rather than enumerating every complete route. In a directed acyclic graph, where edges never loop back, the nodes can be ordered so that every edge goes forward, and the cheapest cost to each node is the minimum over its incoming edges of the neighbor's best cost plus the edge weight. Once every node's best cost is known, the cheapest route to the destination is recovered by walking backward through the choices that achieved those minima. The method replaces exponential route counting with a single pass.

Method. The working method for this record is dynamic programming over a small directed acyclic graph with nodes A through E. First, the edges and their weights are stated, with every edge going forward in alphabetical order so no cycles exist. Second, the best cost to A is set to zero and every other node's best cost starts as unknown. Third, nodes are processed in order, and each node's best cost is computed as the minimum over its incoming edges of the predecessor's best cost plus the edge weight, remembering which predecessor won. Fourth, the destination's best cost is read off and the winning predecessors are followed backward to reconstruct the route. Fifth, the route and its cost are printed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for dynamic programming for shortest route. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: route: A -> C -> E; cost: 7 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a route or schedule forms stages with no cycles, such as project phases, layered networks, or ordered decisions, and when the cheapest total is wanted rather than any workable total. Do not use it where cycles exist without adapting the method, because the ordering it relies on then fails, and do not use it where edge weights change with the route taken. title: Hamming(7,4) Error Correction
body:
Hamming(7,4) error correction is the method for sending four data bits as seven bits so that any single flipped bit can be found and fixed at the receiving end. Three parity bits are woven among the data bits at positions one, two, and four, and each parity bit watches a different overlapping subset of positions. At the receiver, three parity checks are recomputed; when all pass, the data is clean, and when they fail, the pattern of failures, called the syndrome, spells out the position of the flipped bit in binary. Flipping that bit back restores the original seven bits, and the four data bits are read out.

Method. The working method for this record is Hamming(7,4) encoding, corruption, and correction of the data bits one zero one one. First, the data bits are placed at positions three, five, six, and seven, and the three parity bits are computed with even parity over their watched positions. Second, the seven-bit codeword is printed. Third, one bit is flipped to simulate a transmission error. Fourth, the three parity checks are recomputed to form the syndrome, which names the corrupted position. Fifth, that bit is flipped back, the corrected codeword is printed, and the original four data bits are extracted and compared with the input.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for hamming(7,4) error correction. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: codeword: 0110011; received: 0110111; syndrome points at position: 5; corrected: 0110011; data bits: [1, 0, 1, 1] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a channel flips isolated bits and the receiver must repair them without asking for a resend, such as memory systems and deep-space links, which is why Hamming codes remain in real use. Do not use it where two or more bits in one block commonly flip, because single-error correction then misrepairs, and do not use it as encryption, which it is not. def encode(d):
    b = [0] * 8
    b[3], b[5], b[6], b[7] = d
    b[1] = (b[3] + b[5] + b[7]) % 2
    b[2] = (b[3] + b[6] + b[7]) % 2
    b[4] = (b[5] + b[6] + b[7]) % 2
    return b[1:]

def syndrome(b):
    s1 = (b[0] + b[2] + b[4] + b[6]) % 2
    s2 = (b[1] + b[2] + b[5] + b[6]) % 2
    s3 = (b[3] + b[4] + b[5] + b[6]) % 2
    return s3 * 4 + s2 * 2 + s1

data = [1, 0, 1, 1]
code = encode(data)
print('codeword:', ''.join(str(v) for v in code))
corrupt = code[:]
corrupt[4] = 1 - corrupt[4]
print('received:', ''.join(str(v) for v in corrupt))
pos = syndrome(corrupt)
print('syndrome points at position:', pos)
corrupt[pos - 1] = 1 - corrupt[pos - 1]
print('corrected:', ''.join(str(v) for v in corrupt))
print('data bits:', [corrupt[2], corrupt[4], corrupt[5], corrupt[6]])

title: Bicycle Puncture Repair Sequence
body:
Bicycle puncture repair sequence is the ordered procedure for returning a punctured wheel to service, and its value lies in the order as much as in the individual steps. The site of the failure decides the procedure: a tube leak needs the tube found, patched, or replaced; a tire cut needs the tire inspected and protected; a valve leak needs the valve tested and tightened or replaced. Each procedure starts by making the wheel safe to work on, works through inspection before repair so the cause is not missed, and ends with inflation and a check, because a repair that is not checked is only a hope. The same shape, inspect, repair, verify, fits most small mechanical repairs.

Method. The working method for this record is a site-to-procedure mapping with ordered steps. First, the reported site is matched to its procedure: tube, tire, or valve. Second, the steps for that procedure are listed in their working order, starting with wheel removal where needed and ending with inflation and a leak check. Third, each step names its purpose in plain words so a reader can tell whether it has been done properly. Fourth, the demo runs all three sites and prints each procedure's step count and first step, showing that one mapping answers every site. Fifth, the record states that steps must not be reordered, because checking before repair and inflating before checking would both defeat the procedure.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for bicycle puncture repair sequence. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: tube: 7 steps, first step: Remove the wheel; tire: 7 steps, first step: Remove the wheel; valve: 5 steps, first step: Remove the cap Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a bicycle wheel has lost air and the leak's site is known or can be found, and as a template for writing other ordered repair procedures. Do not use it for damage beyond a puncture, such as a bent rim or a torn sidewall that needs professional judgment, and do not ride on a repair that has not passed its final check.
